title: The Real History of Halloween, Told Through a Small Town's Newspapers (Documentary)
alt_titles: Everything You Know About Halloween Is Wrong: The Real History (Documentary)
How a Night of Broken Gates Became Trick-or-Treat: Halloween's Real History
Halloween in Indiana, 1868-2026: What the Old Newspapers Actually Said
description: In 1866, a Philadelphia newspaper described Halloween as the night boys hung dead cats to door-bells. In 1917, an Ontario paper heard gangs shouting "tricks or treats" for the first time. In between, and after, the holiday changed into the one you know.

There was no Celtic god of the dead named Samhain. The church didn't move All Saints' Day to stamp out a pagan festival (the Irish church kept it on April 20). The jack-o'-lantern was a turnip, and the pumpkin version is about 160 years old. Trick-or-treat began as a shakedown. And in nearly 70 years of checking, no child has ever been killed by a stranger's Halloween candy.

This is the history of Halloween as the records show it, stamped MYTH, FACT and NO ONE KNOWS, and the story of what the night looked like in La Porte County, Indiana, from an 1868 shooting over fortune-telling cabbages to the 5-to-7 p.m. trick-or-treat window of today, through the newspapers of the towns around us and the weather records of the nights themselves. (La Porte's own papers from those years are on microfilm at the La Porte County Public Library, not online.)

A La Porte Weather Now documentary. Narrated by a computer voice. The paintings, prints, postcards, photographs, maps, book pages and newspaper pages are real ones, most of them more than a century old; nothing was drawn by AI. Maps and title cards were drawn for the film.

SOURCES

Samhain and All Saints: Ronald Hutton, The Stations of the Sun (Oxford, 1996); Archaeology magazine (Nov.-Dec. 2016) and University College Dublin on the Hill of Ward excavation (Dr. Stephen Davis); Charles Vallancey, A Vindication of the Ancient History of Ireland (1786); the Félire Óengusso and the Martyrology of Tallaght (All Saints on April 20); Encyclopaedia Britannica (1911) on Boniface IV and Gregory III

The words: the Oxford English Dictionary (jack-o'-lantern, 1658/1663/1837; Hallowe'en); Merriam-Webster (Halloween, c. 1700); Alexander Montgomerie, Flyting (1584); Shakespeare, The Two Gentlemen of Verona (1593)

Souling, guising and the games: Lisa Morton, Trick or Treat: A History of Halloween (Reaktion, 2012); Robert Burns, Halloween, in Poems, Chiefly in the Scottish Dialect (Kilmarnock, 1786), with his footnotes; Frank Leslie's Popular Monthly (Nov. 1895); the University of St Andrews Library on the Cupar presbytery (1648)

Stingy Jack and the pumpkin: the Dublin Penny Journal (Jan. 16, 1836); the Daily News, Kingston, Ontario (Nov. 1, 1866); Cindy Ott, Pumpkin: The Curious History of an American Icon (Harper's Weekly, 1867)

American pranks and parties: the Philadelphia Evening Telegraph (Oct. 31, 1866); Godey's Lady's Book (Oct. 1872); the Terre Haute Evening Gazette (Nov. 7, 1872), the Daily Wabash Express (Nov. 3, 1868) and the Terre Haute Express (1889), via the Indiana Historical Bureau, "Devil Cats, Magic Mirrors and Fortune-Telling Cabbage" (2024); the Dictionary of American Regional English (doorbell night, Indianapolis Journal, Nov. 2, 1891); History.com on 1933; Lisa Morton ("buy these kids off")

Northern Indiana: the Whiting-Robertsdale Historical Society (1906, 1909, 1910); the Indiana Historical Bureau's Talking Hoosier History (the Goshen Ghost, 1909); Jeff Kenney, "Spooky Spectacle," Towne Post (2023), quoting the Munster Times (1923) and the Culver Citizen (1950, 1956); the Marion County Historical Society (the 1923 mask ordinance, Indianapolis Star); Mirror Indy (Irvington, 1927); the La Porte County Public Library's "100 Years Ago Today" (1922)

Trick-or-treat: Barry Popik's word files and Wordorigins.org (the Sault Daily Star, Nov. 1, 1917; the Bay City Daily Times, 1928; the Morning Oregonian, 1932; the Helena Independent, 1934; the Los Angeles Times, 1938); War Ration Book One (May 1942) and the end of sugar rationing (June 1947); UNICEF USA (the Allisons, 1950); Peanuts (Oct. 1951); Disney's Trick or Treat (1952)
The candy scare: Joel Best, University of Delaware, "Halloween Sadism" (1985-present); Smithsonian magazine, "Where Did the Fear of Poisoned Halloween Candy Come From?"; The Incidental Economist

Today: the National Retail Federation's 2026 Halloween survey (Sept. 2026); USDA Economic Research Service, pumpkins (2022, 2025); the Hesston Steam Museum; the La Porte County Historical Society; WNDU (2025 trick-or-treat hours); the Washington Park Zoo
Weather: NOAA/National Weather Service records for South Bend (1893-present); NWS Northern Indiana (Oct. 31, 2013 rain); NWS Chicago (Oct. 31, 2014 wind; Oct. 30-31, 2019 snow); ABC57
